newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia's refining growth to spur Mideast oil imports.
newsitem.headline: Asia's refining growth to spur Mideast oil imports.

text.p: Booming refining capacity in the Asia-Pacific region by 1998 will spur higher crude oil imports and lead to greater dependency on Middle East supplies, an oil analyst said on Tuesday.

Asia is expected to add about 1.4 million barrels per day (bpd) to its refining capacity by 1998 and an additional projected capacity of 1.5 million bpd by 2000, said Kang Wu, an oil expert at the East-West Center, a Honolulu-based think-tank.
"Associated with current plans are 1.2 million bpd of planned cracking capacities by 2000, of which about half of the additions will be completed by 1997," Wu told an oil conference.

"The huge and expanding refining capacity in the Asia-Pacific region implies that crude oil will account for most of the oil import dependency, and dependence on the Middle East to supply the region's crude needs will be inescapable."
He said based on the Center's projections, the region's overall crude imports were expected to rise to 66 percent of requirements in 2000, 72 percent in 2005 and 77 percent by 2010.
Wu added that rising refining capacity would also coincide with stagnating crude oil production in the Asia-Pacific region, and this would spur more crude imports from the Middle East.
He said the region's crude output would be moderate but steady over the next few years, reaching 7.2 million bpd in 2000.
Regional crude output would decline to under seven million bpd by 2005 and remain flat thereafter, he said.
Wu said the expansion in refining capacity would cause a marginal drop in Asia's oil products imports from outside the region, but the trend would quickly reverse after 1998.

He said imports of refined products registered 2.2 million bpd in 1995 but would fall to 1.9 million barrels in 1997. The build-up of refining capacity from South Korea, Thailand and China would result in a fall in product imports in the region, he added.
However, by 1998, oil products imports would rise to 2.1 million bpd as booming demand for oil products would then lag expansion in refining capacity, he said.
Over the next 15 years, high average annual growth rates in oil cosumption were expected in Vietnam, the Philippines, India, Pakistan, Thailand, Indonesia, China and Malaysia, he said.
Within the petroleum product categories, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) was forecast to show the fastest growth, followed by diesel, gasoline, kerosene and jet fuel, he said.
The rapidly rising regional demand would also see a decline in crude export availabilities within the Asia-Pacific's oil-producing countries, Wu said.
Regional crude exports were projected to fall from 2.2 million bpd in 1995 to 1.6 million bpd in 2000, he said.
